title: Surtsey, an island that rose out of the sea in 1963, is off-limits to almost everyone
body: An eruption that began 130 m below the sea off Iceland's south coast broke the surface on **14 November 1963**, and a brand-new island started to grow. By the time the eruptions stopped in June 1967, Surtsey covered 2.7 km². Iceland made it a nature reserve while it was still erupting, and today only a few scientists may land there. That way, plants and animals can colonise the bare new rock with no outside interference, and researchers can watch it happen.

cover.alt: Surtsey erupting in 1963, seen from a plane: a huge white steam and ash cloud rising from a dark cone of new land ringed by surf

slides.question: By 2008, how many plant species had been found on Surtsey?
slides.explanation: 69 species had been found, of which about 30 had become established. The first, a sea rocket, turned up on the northern shore in 1965.

events.text: The eruption breaks the surface of the sea
Declared a nature reserve; the first plant appears
Eruptions end, leaving 2.7 km² of land
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

slides.alt: Aerial view of Surtsey today, a small dark island with a pointed spit, surrounded by white surf and deep blue sea
slides.caption: Surtsey seen from the air. Visitors mostly see it like this, from a small plane.

slides.heading: The sea is taking Surtsey back
slides.note: Erosion removes about 1 hectare a year, though its harder core may slow the loss

slides.heading: The tomato that had to go
slides.text: The rules are strict. When a tomato plant took root from human waste that had been badly disposed of, it was destroyed. Birds began nesting about three years after the eruptions ended.

slides.question: Why are only a few scientists allowed to land on Surtsey?
slides.explanation: Keeping people away lets natural ecological succession, the step-by-step arrival of plants and animals, proceed without outside interference.
